Weight refers to how heavy something is, or the force that pulls something downward. Almost every meaning of "weight" branches out from this central idea of heaviness and the effect it has — whether on a physical object, a decision, a person's mind, or a system.
1. How heavy something is (the most common, everyday meaning)

This is what most people mean when they use the word "weight" in daily life. It's the measure of how much an object presses down when placed on a surface.

"The weight of the box is 10 kilograms."
"She gained weight after the holidays."
"The bridge can hold a maximum weight of five tonnes."

Weight is usually measured in kilograms (kg), pounds (lbs), grams (g), tonnes, etc. When you step on a scale, what it shows is your weight.
2. The force of gravity pulling something down (the scientific meaning)

In science — specifically physics — "weight" has a precise meaning that is slightly different from everyday usage.

Weight is a force. It is the gravitational pull that the Earth (or any planet) exerts on an object. The more mass an object has, and the stronger the gravity, the greater its weight.

This is why astronauts on the Moon weigh much less than they do on Earth — the Moon's gravity is weaker. Their mass stays the same, but their weight changes.

In physics, weight is measured in Newtons (N), not kilograms.

"The weight of a 10 kg object on Earth is approximately 98 Newtons."

Weight vs. Mass — an important distinction:

  • Mass is the amount of matter in an object. It never changes, no matter where you are in the universe.
  • Weight is the force of gravity on that mass. It changes depending on where you are.

In everyday conversation, people use "weight" and "mass" interchangeably (saying "I weigh 60 kg"), but strictly speaking, kilograms measure mass, not weight. For everyday purposes, this confusion is harmless, but it's good to know the difference.
3. A heavy object (a physical "weight")

The word "weight" is also used to refer to a physical object that is heavy by design — made to be heavy for a specific purpose.

Gym weights / dumbbells: The heavy metal pieces you lift in a gym.

"He picked up a 10 kg weight and started curling."

Weights on a scale: Small, precisely measured pieces of metal placed on a balance scale to measure how heavy something else is.

"The jeweller used tiny weights to measure the gold."

A paperweight: A small, heavy object placed on papers to stop them from blowing away.

"She kept a glass paperweight on her desk."

A counterweight: A weight placed on one side of a machine or system to balance the other side.

"The crane uses a large counterweight to stay balanced."
4. Importance, influence, or significance

This is one of the most common figurative (non-physical) uses of the word. When something "carries weight," it means it matters, it has power, it has influence on how people think or decide.

"His recommendation carries a lot of weight — people trust his opinion."
"The professor's words had great weight with the students."
"Her evidence gave more weight to the argument."
"The committee gave little weight to his concerns."

Here, "weight" is not about heaviness at all — it's about how seriously something is taken. Just like a heavier object is harder to ignore or move, an important opinion or piece of evidence is harder to dismiss.
5. A burden — something heavy to carry, physically or emotionally

Weight is also used to describe anything that feels like a heavy burden — something that presses down on you, makes life harder, or causes suffering.

Physical burden:

"The weight of the rucksack made hiking exhausting."

Emotional or mental burden:

"She felt the weight of grief after losing her father."
"The weight of responsibility rested on his shoulders."
"He carried the weight of his past mistakes everywhere he went."

The image here is intuitive: just as a heavy physical load is tiring and difficult to bear, so too is an emotional or moral load. We naturally describe difficult feelings and responsibilities using the language of heaviness.
6. The weight of a decision or situation

Closely related to the idea of burden and importance, "weight" can refer to the seriousness or gravity of a situation.

"He paused, feeling the full weight of what he was about to do."
"The judge understood the weight of her decision."
"The weight of the moment was not lost on anyone in the room."

This sense captures how certain moments, choices, or situations feel "heavy" — they demand attention, care, and seriousness.
7. Weight in statistics and data

In mathematics and statistics, a weight is a number assigned to a data point to show how much importance or influence it should have in a calculation.

For example, imagine a student's final grade is calculated like this: exams count more than homework. So exams are given a higher "weight." This is called weighting data.

"Each answer in the survey was given a different weight based on how reliable the source was."
"The weighted average gave more weight to recent data."

The logic is the same as in everyday life: something with more "weight" has more pull, more influence on the final result.
8. Weight in typography and design

In the world of fonts and graphic design, "weight" refers to how thick or thin the strokes of letters are.

"This heading uses a bold weight font."
"The designer chose a light weight for the body text."

You may have seen font options like: Thin, Light, Regular, Medium, Bold, Heavy, Black. These are all different "weights" of the same font. A heavier weight means thicker, bolder letters.
9. Weight in fabric and materials

In textiles and manufacturing, "weight" describes how thick, dense, or heavy a material is per unit of area.

"This winter coat is made from a heavy-weight wool."
"The light-weight cotton is perfect for summer."
"The fabric weight is 200 grams per square metre."

A heavy-weight fabric is thick, warm, and durable. A light-weight fabric is thin, breathable, and easy to move in.
Common phrases and expressions using "weight"

These phrases come up often in English and are worth knowing:

"To pull your weight" — to do your fair share of work.

"Everyone on the team needs to pull their weight."

"To throw your weight around" — to use your power or authority in an aggressive, bossy way.

"The new manager kept throwing his weight around, which upset the staff."

"To throw your weight behind something" — to actively support something with all your influence.

"The senator threw her weight behind the new bill."

"Dead weight" — something (or someone) that is a burden and contributes nothing useful.

"That old machine is just dead weight — it should be thrown away."

"To carry weight" — to be important or credible.

"His long experience in the field carries weight."

"Worth its weight in gold" — extremely valuable.

"A good teacher is worth their weight in gold."

"The weight of the world on one's shoulders" — to feel as though you are responsible for everything and are under enormous pressure.

"After losing the company's biggest client, she felt the weight of the world on her shoulders."

"Under the weight of" — collapsing or struggling because of something heavy — literally or figuratively.

"The old shelf buckled under the weight of the books."
"He crumbled under the weight of expectations."
Putting it all together

The word "weight" is remarkably versatile, but it always comes back to one central idea: heaviness and the effect it has. Whether you are talking about how many kilograms something measures, the gravitational force pulling an object down, a metal disc used for lifting, the seriousness of a decision, the burden of grief, the influence of an opinion, or the thickness of a font — all of these are variations of the same human instinct to describe what is heavy, what presses down, and what demands to be taken seriously.

Understanding this single thread — heaviness as force, burden, and importance — will help you recognise and use "weight" correctly in almost any context you encounter it.
